label: Chapter 7: Two Wars, Expo 58 and the Capital of Europe, 1914 to 1989

units.text: On the fourth of August, 1914, German troops crossed into Belgium.
The German government had offered the Belgians a deal: let our army pass through your country to attack France, and you will be spared.
King Albert the First refused.
The Belgians, he said, would defend their independence.
Germany's chancellor dismissed the neutrality treaty that Germany itself had signed, the treaty of 1839, as nothing more than a scrap of paper.
Britain, which had guaranteed it, declared war.
The Belgian army fought hard, and the German advance was slowed, but it could not be stopped.
On the twentieth of August, German troops marched into Brussels, which had been declared an open city to spare it from destruction.
The occupation would last more than four years.
Brussels lived under German military rule, with curfews, requisitions, food shortages, and harsh punishments.
Meanwhile, King Albert and what was left of the Belgian army held a narrow strip of land in the far west of the country, along the river Yser, for the entire war.
The occupation also gave the city one of its best-known heroines.
Edith Cavell was an English nurse who had come to Brussels in 1907 to run a training school for nurses.

When the war began, she and a network of Belgian and French helpers began hiding Allied soldiers who had been cut off behind enemy lines, and guiding them across the border into the neutral Netherlands.
She is believed to have helped about two hundred men escape.
In August of 1915, the Germans arrested her.
She openly admitted what she had done.
She was tried, sentenced to death, and on the twelfth of October, 1915, shot by a firing squad, in the early morning, at a shooting range in the Brussels suburb of Schaerbeek.
Her execution caused an outcry around the world.
The night before, she told a chaplain that patriotism was not enough, and that she must have no hatred or bitterness toward anyone.
The war ended in November of 1918, and on the twenty-second of that month King Albert rode into a liberated Brussels.
The next two decades were a time of recovery and glamor.
Art Deco buildings appeared across the city.
The great Palais des Beaux-Arts, designed by Victor Horta, opened in 1928.

In 1927, the physicist community gathered in Brussels for the fifth Solvay Conference, where the leading scientists of the age, including Einstein, Bohr, Marie Curie, Heisenberg, and Schrödinger, debated the strange new science of quantum mechanics.
The surrealist painter René Magritte lived and worked in the city.

And a young Brussels cartoonist named Georges Remi, who signed his work Hergé, published the first adventure of a young reporter with a quiff of red hair in a children's supplement of a newspaper in January of 1929.
Belgium's comic strip tradition, which would make Brussels a world capital of the form, had begun.
Then, once again, the Germans came.
On the tenth of May, 1940, they invaded Belgium.
King Leopold the Third, who had succeeded his father Albert, surrendered the army eighteen days later, against the wishes of his government, which went into exile in London.
The king stayed in Belgium as a prisoner.
That decision would split the country for years afterward.
Brussels was occupied for four years.
Resistance networks sprang up, helping Allied airmen to escape, hiding Jewish children, and publishing underground newspapers.
But the occupation was brutal.

Tens of thousands of Belgians were sent to forced labor in Germany, and about twenty-five thousand Jews, most of them from Brussels and Antwerp, were deported to the death camps through a transit camp in the city of Mechelen.
Only a small fraction survived.
Many Belgian families risked their lives hiding Jewish neighbors.
Liberation came on the third of September, 1944, when British tanks of the Guards Armoured Division rolled into Brussels to scenes of overwhelming joy.
Compared to many other European cities, Brussels came through the war relatively unscathed.
Its buildings were mostly intact, and its position in the center of Western Europe was about to become its destiny.
But first, the country had to settle the question of the king.
After the war, many Belgians, especially in Wallonia and in Brussels, wanted to punish Leopold the Third for his surrender and for some of his actions during the occupation.
Others, mostly in Catholic Flanders, defended him.

In 1950, a referendum showed that a majority of Belgians wanted him back, but the split followed the language line almost perfectly: strong support in Flanders, and a majority against him in Wallonia and in Brussels.
Strikes, riots, and violence followed.
In 1951, Leopold abdicated in favor of his twenty-year-old son, Baudouin, to calm the country.
It was an early sign of how deeply the language divide could cut.
In the postwar years, Belgium chose a very different path from its prewar neutrality.
It became a founding member of NATO in 1949 and of the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951.
And a Belgian socialist politician, Paul-Henri Spaak, became one of the leading architects of European unity.
In 1955 and 1956, Spaak chaired the committee that wrote the report that led to the Treaties of Rome of 1957, creating the European Economic Community, the ancestor of today's European Union.
When the new community needed a home for its executive, the Commission, it was set up in Brussels in 1958, intended as a temporary arrangement.
It never left.
That same year, 1958, Brussels hosted the first world's fair after the Second World War.
Expo 58 opened in April on the Heysel plateau, on the northern edge of the city, and it was meant to show a confident new age of science and peace.
The pavilions of the United States and the Soviet Union stood across from each other, in the middle of the Cold War.

And at the center was the most striking structure of all: the Atomium, a giant model of an iron crystal, magnified about a hundred and sixty-five billion times, made of nine shining steel spheres linked by tubes, rising a hundred and two meters into the air.
It was supposed to be demolished after the fair, but Brusselers loved it too much.
It is now the most recognizable symbol of the city.
Then came 1960, and the end of an empire.
On the thirtieth of June, 1960, the Belgian Congo became independent.

At the ceremony, King Baudouin praised Belgium's colonial work, and Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the new country, gave an angry reply about the humiliations and brutality of colonial rule.
Within months, the Congo collapsed into crisis, and in January of 1961, Lumumba was murdered.
Decades later, a Belgian parliamentary commission concluded that Belgian officials bore a moral responsibility for his death, and the Belgian government apologized in 2002.
In 2022, Belgium returned a tooth, a relic of his remains, to his family.
The 1960s were also the decade when Brussels began to look like the capital of Europe.
In 1967, NATO moved its political headquarters from Paris to Brussels, after the French president, Charles de Gaulle, withdrew France from the alliance's military command.
The European Commission moved into a huge, star-shaped office building called the Berlaymont, finished in 1967.
A whole district of offices spread across the eastern side of the city, around the Rue de la Loi.
This building boom had a cost.
In the 1960s and 1970s, developers and the government tore down entire neighborhoods and many fine old buildings to make room for offices, highways, and towers.
One of the most painful losses was Victor Horta's Maison du Peuple, a masterpiece of Art Nouveau, demolished in 1965 despite protests.
The destruction became so notorious that a new word was invented, Bruxellisation, meaning the careless, speculative destruction of a historic city.
By the late 1960s, citizens' groups fought back and began to protect the old districts.
The metro opened in 1976, and the city started, slowly, to be more careful with its past.
And all the while, the question of language and region was growing hotter.
In 1962 and 1963, Belgium fixed a border between its Dutch-speaking and French-speaking areas, and Brussels was left as a bilingual island inside Flemish territory.
In 1968, the great Catholic university in Leuven split in two, along language lines.
Over the next two decades, a series of constitutional reforms gradually turned Belgium from a centralized country into a federation of regions and language communities.
In 1989, the third region took shape: the Brussels-Capital Region, made up of nineteen municipalities, officially bilingual.
In 1993, Belgium formally became a federal state.
If you want to see this chapter, take the metro to Schuman station.
Walk out and you will face the Berlaymont, with its star-shaped wings, the headquarters of the European Commission.
Nearby is the Cinquantenaire park, where Leopold the Second's arch stands.
And if you have time for a trip to the north end of the city, the Atomium is still there, with a view from the top sphere over the whole region.
In the final chapter, we come to the Brussels of today.
